NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE AUTHORITY (NHIA)
FOREWORD
The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) remains committed to achieving financial access to quality
healthcare for all Nigerians. As part of this commitment, the Authority continuously strengthens healthcare
delivery through policies, frameworks, and operational tools that enhance the efficiency, quality, and
standardization of services provided under the NHIA ecosystem. The review of the Standard Treatment
Guidelines and Referral Protocol (STGRP) for Primary Care represents a critical step in this direction.
This revised STRP reflects the latest evidence-based clinical best practices, ensuring a more structured,
ational, and efficient approach to treatment and referrals within NHIA-accredited facilities. This edition align
vith the NHIA's strategic objectives of expanding coverage, enhancing equity, improving quality and ensurin
market efficiency as critical pillars for advancing Universal Health Coverage in Nigeria. With this update, the
Authority seeks to furnish healthcare providers with a user-friendly, standardized, and practical decision-
making tool that supports the accurate and timely identification of health conditions, appropriate treatment
interventions, and seamless referral pathways.
Additionally, this version of the STGRP is harmonized with numerous national policies for disease

local, subnational, national and international current best practices on accurate diagnosis and treatment,

ABOUT THIS STANDARD TREATMENT GUIDELINE AND REFERRAL PROTOCOL / HOW TO USE IT
The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) decided to review its 2023 Standard Treatment Guide and
Referral Protocol (STGRP) for primary health care providers in all its accredited primary health care facilities
for the delivery of medical and health services to enrolees. The PHC may be stand-alone or part of a hospital,
publicly owned or private. The clinicians in PHC in Nigeria include family physicians, general practitioners,
medical officers, nurses, midwifes, community health officers (CHO), community health extension workers
(CHEW), junior community health extension workers (JCHEW). Other practitioners that will use the STGRP,
as appropriate, include pharmacists, physical therapists, and various technicians. Therefore, Referral in the
STGRP connotes transfer of care of a patient from one clinician to another, often a higher-level facility, or to
another section within the same facility, following the recommendations in the Guide.
The STGRP is not a Textbook. It is designed to facilitate the Consultation and Referral Process and Steps
as the various cadres of provider-clinicians attend to patents in the setting of ever-busy PHCs. The user
applies basic and contemporary consultation principles of patient-centred care, in context, which consists of:
defining the patient's true agenda (why have they come today?), and main complaint, eliciting and considering
other problems very early-on in the consultation, choosing an appropriate action for each problem, achieving
a shared understanding with the patient, using time and resources appropriately, and establishing and
maintaining a professional relationship with the patient. For ease-of-use, the disease chapters are arranged
alphabetically, whilst the conditions within each chapter are arranged according to how commonly they
present in PHC in Nigeria.
Each chapter has a brief description of the disease/condition under the
Introduction. The design of the guide also emphasizes the importance of eliciting the patient's ideas and
concerns about their complaint, and their expectations from the clinician/provider by asking open questions
such as 'Was there anything else you were hoping to discuss today?', 'What is your main fear/worry/concern
about your problem?', and 'What were you hoping to get out of today's visit to the health centre?'. This is
followed by appropriate and adequate physical examination, requesting relevant investigations only, and
shared decision making about the treatment that the provider wants to recommend. This is only possible if
the provider has shared his / her working diagnosis with the patient, including the benefit of the treatment
and any known side effects. Where referral is decided, the reason should be explained to the enrollee /
patient and parent/ guardian (in the case of the under-age or mentally ill patients). The STGRP has been
written, as far as possible, in simple English Language to aid understanding and clarity, user-friendliness,
and to enhance confidence of the provider. Where the patient is acutely ill and will be referred to the hospital,
as appropriate, this protocol provides the clinician with essential interventions to stabilise the patient before
he / she is transferred, so that they begin to experience some relief, and do not deteriorate during the journey
to the hospital. It is hoped that by ensuring uniformity of care across the PHC facilities in the country, this
protocol increases the acceptability of and confidence in the NHIA and health system. It also makes it possible
to conduct robust training on how to use the STGRP, supportive supervision, mentoring, monitoring, and
evaluation of the use of the protocol, to ensure that the aims/objectives of the protocol are achieved by its
use.
Every referral should follow the referral protocol steps, and every referred patient should be given a fully
completed referral form as the proceed to the referral hospital/centre.
THIS STRGRP DOES NOT REPLACE CLINICAL JUDGEMENT AND EXPERIENCE OF PROVIDERS /
USERS/CLINICIANS -
The provider-clinician who uses this protocol must ensure best practice by eliciting vital information from the
observation of the patient, the history, physical examination, sufficient to make a good and informed-working-
18

NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE AUTHORITY (NHIA)
diagnosis, ordering only necessary tests where indicated, that will guide the recommended treatment/
management. The STGRP does not restrict the user/provider from applying his / her clinical
judgement when attending to the patient in their presence, and who they should manage drawing
from their training, re-training and practice according to their limit, license and competency, which
they must not exceed.
USING THIS STANDARD TREATMENT GUIDELINE AND REFFERAL PROTOCOL: GUIDE TO
CLINICIAN-PROVIDERS
For ease-of-use, the disease chapters are arranged alphabetically, whilst the conditions within each chapter
are arranged according to how commonly they present in PHC in Nigeria. The provider-clinician as he / she
takes a good and full history to establish the main and other complaints of the patient, should confirm from
the patient, then find the main complaint heading in the content pages of the STRP, and then turn to the
page. The clinician shall continue to ask all / as many as necessary questions as are listed in the history
box/column, and more, if considered useful; then conduct appropriate physical examination as listed in the
various boxes, before requesting only relevant investigations. The clinician-provider shall always ensure that
any emergency resuscitation measures that are necessary for the particular patient, are carried out, promptly,
before the patient is put on the transport for transfer to the referral hospital. Gathering and documenting all
significant patient history/information, including negative ones, is sacrosanct in medical practice, for example,
in the examination of a "painful abdomen", if there is no tenderness on examination, the clinician should
record in patient's notes: "no abdominal tenderness".
". The next step in using this protocol is to review the list
of findings, locate the recommended action (s) as they correspond to the selected group of findings, and
manage the patient as stated in the protocol. If the patient is to be referred, stabilize the patient first, as he /
she awaits transfer. For example, 'administer a painkiller to a patient who is in pain awaiting transfer", or set
up an I.V. line for fluid/drip if patient is dehydrated or is advised not to take anything by mouth until they see
the clinician in the referral centre, etc. In all of these actions, the clinician-provider must not exceed his / her
competence/level.
This demands that the attending physician or other health worker must refer patients to the next higher level
of care as appropriate and without delay, and to aid this process, a column for RED FLAGS has been created
where indications for referral are listed to prompt the primary health care clinician-provider to refer.
A page is created for the Referral Protocol Steps to be followed for every referral and the Referral Form which
must be completed for every referred patient has also been included in this STGRP. Follow the recognized
recommendations on medicines / drugs, for rational prescribing, use and administration. If referral is delayed,
and a course of medicine or injection which you have started, is due to finish, review the patient, give the
next dose if the time is due for the next dose. This is good continuity of care practice for a patient still under
your charge. All patients are entitled to respect, dignity, privacy, informed consent and confidentiality as they
receive care. These fundamental tenets must be observed. There is no substitute to accurate and clear
documentation of history, findings, tests, treatment, and counselling given to the patient, with date and time
and name/signature of the provider, legibly written. The documentation must be contemporaneous, that is
written at the time the patient is attended to, not days or weeks after.

WRITING A PRESCRIPTION PROPERLY
Delegation, task shifting and sharing the prescribing function from medical doctors who are the traditional
prescribers, to other cadres in the health team including, nurses, midwives, community health practitioners
(i.e CHO/CHEW/JCHEW), pharmacists, has come to stay in present-day running of health facilities, and it
therefore makes this chapter essential, to ensure proper, rational prescribing that reduces catastrophic
consequences of wrongly written prescriptions for the patient. The aim is to control or even eliminate improper
prescribing. All drugs are potentially harmful to a patient and therefore prescriptions should be written by
medical doctors and dentists (traditional Prescribers - MP), and by non-medical prescribers (NMP) when
carrying out the delegated task, often to cover the shortage of medical and dental personnel. NMPs may be
permitted by the ministry of health / relevant authority to prescribe according to their limit of training,
competence and capacity as they deliver patient care, usually prescribing from a limited list of medicines,
and under supervision of the traditional medical prescribers. The following points are essential and should
be followed when writing a prescription for a patient. A prescriber must ensure to write on the prescription
form (not on pieces / scraps of paper): The management of the health facility should provide proper
prescription forms/pads for use by authorized prescribers (MP and NMP) in the facilities:
1. Write Directions, preferably in English without abbreviation. If necessary, use the abbreviations listed
in the STGRP. Avoid the use of other abbreviations.
2. Write Patients Biodata and address in full (name, age, date of birth, gender (Male/Female), etc). Fill-
in / complete ALL spaces on the prescription form!
3. Write Name of medicines and the preparation / formulation to be taken / or given in full.
4. Unofficial abbreviations should not be used because of high risk of misinterpretation by those
dispensing for or administering the drug to the patient.
5. Non-proprietary (i.e. generic) names in the prescription.
6. Quantities of 1 gram or more should be written 1 g.
7. Quantities less than 1 gram should be written in milligrams, e.g. 500 mg, and not 0.5 g.
8. Quantities less than 1mg should be written in micrograms, e.g. 100 micrograms, not 0.1 mg.
9. Micrograms' and 'nanograms' should not be abbreviated. Similarly, 'units' should not be abbreviated.
25

NATIONALHEALTHINSURANCE AUTHORITY (NHIA)
10. Avoid the unnecessary use of decimal points, e.g. write 3 mg and not 3.0 mg.
11. Where decimals are unavoidable, a zero should be written in front of the decimal point where there
is no other figure, e.g. 0.5 ml, and not .5ml
12. Use the term 'millilitre' (ml or mL) not cubic centimetre (cc, Or cm3).
13. State dose and dose frequency. Where medications are to be given 'as required', a minimum dose
interval should be specified, e.g. 'every 4-6 hrs as required for pain'.
14. State the quantity to be supplied or indicate the number of days of treatment required.
15. Avoid combination drugs, unless there is evidence of a significant therapeutic advantage over single
ingredient preparations (e.g. Co-trimoxazole).
16. Avoid the use of symptomatic treatments for minor self-limiting conditions. Treat the diagnosis,
unless when not known yet.
17. Avoid prescribing placebos. Instead, spend some time educating and reassuring the patient.
18. Avoid multiple prescribing (polypharmacy), especially when the diagnosis is not clear.
19. Avoid the use of the parenteral route of administration, except where there are clear, clinical
indications for this route. Use the oral route whenever possible.
ADVISE THE PATIENT NEEDING A PRESCRIPTION
• Explain to the patient why the medication is needed, what effect it will have and what will happen if it is taken
incorrectly.
• Explain to the patient when and how to take the medication and for how long. Ask the patient to repeat your
explanation to ensure s/he understands.
• Educate the patient on the importance of adherence and that not adhering to medication may lead to relapse
or worsening of the condition and possible resistance to the medication.
• Advise the patient of possible side effects to the medication and what to do if they occur.
• Over-the-counter medications and herbal treatments may interfere with prescribed medication. Encourage
patient to discuss with prescriber before using them.

PROTECT YOURSELF FROM OCCUPATIONAL INFECTION
If a health worker has a sharps injury or splash on the eye, mouth, nose or broken skin from one or more of the following,
treat as urgent case:
Blood, Blood-stained fluid/tissue, pleural/pericardial/peritoneal/amniotic/synovial/cerebrospinal
fluid, vaginal
secretions, semen, or breast milk,
Management: 1) If broken skin, clean area immediately with soap and water. 2) If splash to eye, mouth or nose,
immediately rinse mouth/nose or irrigate eye thoroughly with water or sodium chloride (0.9%). 3) If a health worker
has had contact with viral haemorrhagic fever (Lassa Fever, Ebola, COVID-19, etc) suspect, refer hospital urgently.
4) Assess need for HIV and hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis.
Recommended actions to prevent risk of occupation-related infection:
Personal Protection - BEFORE SEEING EVERY PATIENT APPLY STANDARD PRECAUTIONS, including: 1) Wash hands
with soap/water or use alcohol-based cleaner after contact with patients orbody fluids. 2) Dispose of sharps correctly
in sharps bins. Wear protective gear: 1) Wear gloves when handling blood, body fluids, secretions or non-intact skin. 2)
Wear face mask if in contact with respiratory virus suspects (N95 respirator if TB suspect). 3) Wear a face mask with a visor
or glasses if at risk of splashes. 4) Wear personal protective equipment if in contact with viral haemorrhagic fever suspects
(Lassa Fever, Ebola, COVID-19, etc). GET VACCINATED: Get vaccinated against hepatitis B, Tetanus, Covid-19, others.
ENSURE TO KNOW YOUR HIV STATUS: 1) Test for HIV. ART and IPT can decrease the risk of TB. 2) If HIV positive, you
are entitled to work in an area of the facility where exposure to TB is limited.
Facility Protection includes - Manage infection control in the facility: Appoint an infection control officer for the facility to
coordinate and monitor infection control policies. Organize waiting areas: 1) Prevent overcrowding in waiting areas. 2)
Fast track TB suspects. Clean the facility: 1) Clean frequently touched surfaces (door handles, telephones, keyboards) daily
with soap and water. Disinfect surfaces contaminated with blood/secretions with 70% alcohol or chlorine-based
disinfectant. Manage sharps safely: Ensure sharps bins are easily accessible and regularly replaced
Manage occupational exposure promptly:
Beware and reduce TB risk - Identify TB suspects promptly: 1) The patient with cough ≥ 2 weeks is a TB suspect. 2) Separate
TB suspect from others in the facility. 3) Educate about cough hygiene and give face mask/tissues to cover mouth/nose
to protect others. Diagnose TB rapidly: Fast track TB workup and start treatment as soon as diagnosed. To protect yourself
from TB by: Wear an N95 respirator (not a face mask) if in contact with an infectious TB patient.
Reduce risk of respiratory viruses: 1) Wash hands with soap and water. 2) Wear a face mask over mouth and nose during
procedures on patient. 2) Encourage patients to cover mouth/ nose with a tissue when coughing/sneezing, to dispose
of used tissues correctly and to wash hands regularly with running water/soap. 3) Advise patients to avoid close contact
with others, until symptom controlled/cured

NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE AUTHORITY (NHIA)
PROTECT YOURSELF FROM OCCUPATIONAL STRESS
Present day work environment is stressful, therefore experiencing some pressure and demands from
patients and colleagues and the employer at work is normal. However, personal and corporate efforts must be
made to keep these demands in control and manageable to prevent / reduce burn-out. The personal ability to
cope with occupational stress is very important for well-being and performance
A Health worker with occupational stress and the following should be treated urgently and referred to mental
health services: 1) Alcohol or drug intoxication at work. 2) Aggressive or violent behaviour at work. 3)
Inappropriate behaviour at work. 4) Suicidal thoughts or behaviour.
To prevent burnt-out and reduce risk of occupational stress, the following interventions are important:
Self-Protection: 1) Look after your health: (Get enough sleep; Exercise, eat sensibly, minimise alcohol and do NOT
smoke; Get screened for chronic conditions.). 2) Look after your chronic condition if you have one: (Adhere to your
treatment and your appointments; Don't diagnose and treat yourself; If you can, confide in a trusted colleague/manager)
3) Manage stress: ( Talk to someone (friend, psychologist, mentor; Spend time with supportive friends or family; Find time
for exercise each day; at work, delegate more, but monitor those you delegate to). 4) Have healthy work-life balanced
habits: (Manage your time sensibly; Take scheduled breaks.; Be sure you are clear about your role and responsibilities;
Remind yourself of your purpose as a health worker).
Protect your team, be a team player: 1) Decide on an approved way of behaving at work: (Treat colleagues and patients
with respect; Instead of complaining, rather focus on finding solutions to problems; Support each other. Consider setting
up a staff support group.; Lean to communicate effectively with your patients and colleague); 2) Learn to cope with stressful
events: (Develop procedures to deal with events like complaints, harassment/bullying, accidents/mistakes, violence or death
of patient or staff member.); 3) Look at how to make the job less stressful: (Support each other to develop skills to
better perform your role; Discuss each team member's role. Ensure each one has say in how she does his/her work; if
possible, examine the team's workload to see if it can be better streamlined; Identify what needs to be changed to make
the job easier and frustrations fewer: equipment, drug supply, training, space, décor in work environment.) 4) Reward and celebrate:
(Acknowledge the achievements of individuals and the team; be part of organising or participating in team social events.).
Identify occupational stress in yourself and your colleagues: 1) Change in mood e.g. Indifferent, tense, irritable or angry;
felt down, depressed, hopeless or 2) felt little interest or pleasure in doing things? If yes to ), 2) Poor Attendance at work
3) Marked decline in work performance e.g. fatigue, poor concentration 4) Recent distressing event e.g. diagnosis of
chronic ilness, bereavement, traumatic event, needle stick injury. 5) Alcohol or other drug problem e.g. drinking more than 4
drinks / session; used illegal drugs; misused prescription or over-the-counter medicines; smell of alcohol

MALARIA
Malaria is a life-threatening infection contacted by humans from bite by some types of mosquitoes. It is mostly found in tropical countries, like Nigeria. It is preventable and curable.
Symptoms can be mild or life-threatening. Mild symptoms are fever, chills and headache. Severe symptoms include fatigue, confusion, seizures, and difficulty breathing. Infants,
children under 5 years, pregnant women and girls, travellers and people with HIV or AIDS are at higher risk of severe infection. Malaria can be prevented by avoiding mosquito
bites and with medicines. Treatments can stop mild cases from getting worse. The infection is caused by a parasite and does not spread from person to person.'

TRAUMA & INJURIES
Trauma is defined as a tissue injury that occurs more or less suddenly due to violence or accident. It initiates hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and immunologic and metabolic
responses responsible for restoring disrupted homeostasis. Trauma can be categorized broadly into 3 groups: penetrating, blunt, and deceleration trauma. There is a significant
overlap in the causes, outcomes, and body's response to the different injury types. A traumatic injury occurs when a person is suddenly hurt and has serious injuries like bleeding,
broken bones or head injuries, which leads to the common sequela of the body's autonomic nervous system activation. Note that each person responds differently to trauma, and
any underlying chronic medical conditions (co-morbidity) can alter normal physiologic responses. Another entity, trauma-induced coagulopathy, can present in trauma patients.

APPENDIX 2: INTRAVENOUS REHYDRATION FOR CHILDREN
INDICATIONS:
• Current evidence suggests nasogastric rehydration (NGTR) is safer and more effective but IV
rehydration is indicated for severe dehydration and if NGTR fails (eg. ongoing profuse losses or
abdominal pain).
Also suitable for children who already have an IV in situ.
Certain comorbidities, particularly GIT conditions (eg. short gut or previous gut surgery) - discuss
these patients with senior staff.
IV Fluids see guideline:
• If shocked: 20ml/kg 0.9% sodium chloride (normal saline) boluses, repeated until shock is
corrected.
Measure blood glucose and treat hypoglycaemia with 5ml/kg of 10% glucose.
• Rapid IV Rehydration: In older children > 4 years with moderate dehydration with no
comorbidities, no electrolyte disturbance and no significant abdominal pain, consider 10 ml/kg/hr
(up to 1000ml/hr) for 4 hours of Plasma-Lyte 148 and 5% Glucose OR 0.9% sodium chloride
(normal saline) and 5% Glucose, then reassess.
Standard IV Rehydration: Otherwise, rehydrate at the rates in Table 4 below for the first 24 hours.
Use Plasma-Lyte 148 and 5% Glucose OR 0.9% sodium chloride (normal saline) and 5%
Glucose for rehydration after any required boluses. If serum K < 3mmol/L, add KCI 20mmol/L, or
give oral supplements.
Measure Na, K and glucose at the outset and at least 24 hourly from then on (more frequent
testing is indicated for patients with comorbidities or if more unwell). Venous blood gases provide
rapid results. It is not necessary to send an electrolyte tube to the lab unless measurement of urea
or creatinine is clinically indicated
• Consider septic work-up or surgical consult in severely unwell patients with gastroenteritis.

APPENDIX 4: CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE (CVD) RISK CALCULATION AND CARE
CVD risk is the chance of having a heart attack or stroke over the next 10 years
Identify if the patient has established CVD:
• Patient known with any of: previous heart attack, angina or heart failure, previous stroke or TIA or
peripheral vascular disease.
• If patient has current/recent chest pain, especially on exertion and relieved by rest, screen for ischaemic
heart disease.
• If patient has current/recent leg pain, especially on walking and relieved by rest, screen for peripheral
vascular disease.
• If new sudden asymmetric weakness or numbness of face, arm or leg; difficulty speaking or visual
disturbance: consider stroke or TIA.
Look for CVD risk factors:
• Ask about smoking: consider the patient who quit smoking in the past year a smoker for CVD risk
assessment.
• Ask about family history: a parent or sibling with premature CVD (man < 55 years or woman < 65
years) is a risk factor.
• Calculate Body Mass Index (BMI): weight (kg) ÷ height (m) ÷ height (m). A BMI > 25 is a risk factor.
• Measure waist circumference over no/light clothing, at the end of a normal breath out, midway between
lowest rib and top of iliac crest. More than 80cm (woman) or 94cm (man) is a risk factor.
• Look for hypertension: check BP.
• Look for diabetes: check glucose.
• Check random total cholesterol. If unavailable, use cholesterol of 5.2mmol/L to calculate CVD risk.
Calculate the patient's CVD risk:
• Plot patient's risk on charts' below using diabetes status, age, sex, systolic BP (SBP), cholesterol and
smoking status. Show the patient what his/her risk of heart attack or stroke might be over next 10 years.

APPENDIX 15: READY-TO-USE THERAPEUTIC FOOD (RUTF) REFERENCE TABLE
Key Messages
• Ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) is a food and medicine for severely malnourished individuals.
It should not be shared
• Sick children often don't like to eat. Give small amounts of RUTF regularly and encourage the child
to eat often until the day's ration is finished.
• RUTF should never be added to or mixed with porridge or any other food.
• Your child should have (x) packets a day.
• For young children, continue breastfeeding on demand. Always breastfeed fully before giving the
child RUTF.
• Always give the child RUTF after breastfeeding but before other food, including corn-soy blend.
• Always give the child plenty of breast milk or safe water to drink while eating RUTF. Children will
need to drink more than normal.
• Use soap to wash the child's hands and ensure that the child is clean before feeding. Keep food
clean and covered.
Children who are malnourished get cold quickly. Always keep the child covered and warm.
Do not stop feeding when the child has diarrhoea. Refer children with diarrhoea for clinical
assessment. Increase the frequency of breastfeeding. After feeding the child RUTE, give him/her
extra clean water.

APPENDIX 16: ALBENDAZOLE FORMS, STRENGTHS, AND DOSES
• 400 mg tablet
Dosage and duration
Ascariasis, enterobiasis, hookworm infections: Child over 6 months and adult: 400 mg single dose;
Child over 6 months but under 10 kg: 200 mg single dose; In the event of enterobiasis, a second dose
may be given after 2 to 4 weeks.
Trichuriasis, strongyloidiasis: Child over 6 months and adult: 400 mg once daily for 3 days; Child over
6 months but under 10 kg: 200 mg once daily for 3 days
Trichinellosis: Child over 2 years: 5 mg/kg 2 times daily for 10 to 15 days; Adult: 400 mg 2 times daily for
10 to 15 days
Contra-indications, adverse effects, precautions:
• Do not administer to children under 6 months.
• Do not administer to patients with ocular cysticercosis.
• May cause: i. gastrointestinal disturbances, headache, dizziness. ii. neurological disorders
(headache, seizures) in patients with undiagnosed neuro cysticercosis.
• Pregnancy: avoid during the first trimester
• Breast-feeding: no contra-indication
Remarks:
• Tablets are to be chewed or crushed: follow manufacturer's recommendations.
• In the treatment of strongyloidiasis, ivermectin is more effective than albendazole.
• Albendazole is also used in the treatment of cutaneous larva migrans (Ancylostoma
braziliense and caninum), larval cestode infections (hydatid disease, certain forms of
neurocysticercosis) and in mass treatment for lymphatic filariasis (check national recommendations).

APPENDIX 20: ORAL REHYDRATION SOLUTION (ORS):
HOW TO PREPARE
A. IF ORAL REHYDRATION SALT SACHET (ORS) NOT AVAILABLE:
Add half a teaspoon (2.5g) salt and 6 teaspoons (30g) sugar to 1 litre of safe water. Give as
much as prescribed.
B. IF ORAL DEHYDRATION SALT SACHET (ORS) AVAILABLE:
Dissolve the contents of one sachet in 1000mls (Two 50cl Fanta/coke bottles) of
clean pre-boiled water. The child or adult should drink as much of it as he wants. If
the child vomits, the mother should wait for about 10 minutes and give it again.
C. The addition of zinc to oral rehydration solution has been proven effective in children with
acute diarrhoea in developing countries and is recommended by the WHO.

APPENDIX 21A: STANDARD DRUG REGIMENS FOR ADULTS WITH TB
A. Six-month regime
• Initial Intensive Phase: This is for two months using Rifampicin (R), Isoniazid (I),
Pyrazinamide (P) and Ethambul (E)
• Continuation Phase: This is for 4 months using Isoniazid, and Rifampicin. Pyridoxine
10mg is usually added to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
In this regimen, there is fully supervised administration of drugs in both intensive and
continuation phases.
For those who do not become negative after 2-month intensive phase, their treatment
is extended by another 2 months.
